content:
Thank you for this essay. There is much in it that resonates positively with me. There are some aspects that don't. For example the passage "We can't rely on anyone else to figure it out.." seems to underestimate the mathematical talent of the computer scientists and employees of big tech companies. (I do agree with the premise that "We (professional and other mathematicians) shouldn't rely ...")

The paragraph containing the phrase "This is the real sense in which we are in danger ..." is alarmist in tone, and I suspect is more alarmist than it should be. Dialing it back, it should be realized that mathematics itself won't disappear or be completely disregarded; it is more likely that the emphasis and importance will be diminished, which will in turn have some consequences for the field of mathematics and its practitioners, but these consequences are not extinction-level. (I do agree that mathematics should maintain or increase its current level of relevance and application, and that professional mathematicians are not doing enough in this direction in the current situation. I don't agree that all of humanity will fall out of love with mathematics and leave the subject to wither and die.)

I like the paragraph beginning "Perhaps even more important are the values..". When you write the companion essay which talks about what mathematics was and what it is now and what your ideas of how it will evolve, you should rewrite this paragraph to include not only the positive aspects of the values and attitudes, but also the negative ones. I think for the field and the body of practitioners to evolve in a healthy fashion, all aspects of the values and attitudes should be considered.

Regarding the paragraph starting "Our discipline has not been kind to them.", I largely agree with it. However, I think it could be more carefully phrased, perhaps mollified by saying "count for little" and "much of the mathematical establishment".

I suggest that a more expository and connective approach be adopted for future mathematics. Practitioners (professional or not) should focus on explaining and connecting a subject to others as much or more than developing results and proofs in a subject. Newer perspectives should be presented on old subjects, and the technology can help here by suggesting simpler and different (possibly better) analogies for explaining a topic. There should also be more emphasis on methods and patterns, and their appearance across different fields; this is a signal that shouts on more effective and more far-reaching research. Technology can help with this too. If we do a good job, we can bring mathematics to more of humanity and increase the level of appreciation of the field: I see improved exposition and new perspectives as necessary here.

I look forward to your future essay on future mathematics, and what more you think should be changed for the field and its practitioners to develop.
sender_full_name: J. J. Issai (project started by GRP)

content: A message was moved here from #General announcements > essay on AI for mathematics by Julian Berman.

I was finishing grad school around the time the blockchain craze hit, and I watched a lot of otherwise smart people fall for the hype of a useless technology. LLMs have been slightly less useless, but nothing I’ve seen so far strikes me as fundamentally revolutionary. If they could stop cheating and hallucinating, that might be something. But it’s still ultimately an elaborate Mechanical Turk.

Disclaimer: I'm a computer scientist, not a mathematician.

I think that trying to belittle these LLMs is, while self-assuring, quite naive.
An year ago, I would agree with the "Mechanical Turk" part. But after seeing these systems generalize, reason through, debug, attack and fix highly non-trivial software, I've completely changed my mind.

I've used such AI systems to help me with mathematics several times. And it never failed to explain things to me more cleanly and patiently than the vast majority of the professors I've had. But to be honest, the thing that amazes me the most is... basic euclidean geometry.

For example, take this simple problem I've just come up with:

Suppose an equilateral triangle ABCABCABC is inscribed in a circle Γ\GammaΓ. The angle bisectors from BBB and CCC, together with side BCBCBC, form a smaller triangle inside ABCABCABC. A circle Γ′\Gamma'Γ′ is inscribed in this smaller triangle. What is the ratio of the area of Γ′\Gamma'Γ′ to the area of Γ\GammaΓ?

I asked ChatGPT and Deepseek and both nailed it almost instantly.
But they don’t reason. It is impressive that LLMs can mimic understanding natural language, but it’s just mimicry by brute computation. What’s interesting about that?

I would not be able to technically define what it is to reason, so I won't talk about that part of your message (which pertains to very interesting philosophical questions though).

From what I understand of LLMs, which is admittedly little, they do not perform brute force computation. Instead, they seem to make highly sophisticated guesses and try a few of them out. Brute force would collect together a huge amount of guesses and try every one of them.

What is interesting, in my opinion, is that LLMs are able to perform tasks (often imperfectly, granted) which so far required highly trained human beings. Of course, you have the examples of resolving of conjectures, but also (quite efficient) interactive mechanisation of maths and the more impressive automechanisation of non-trivial results. From a pragmatic standpoint, this is very interesting, as these tasks could clearly not be done in this way by previous tools.
By brute computation I mean the “large” in large-language model. Feeding tons of training data into a black box and turning a crank.

Agreed, it needs a lot of data for training and behaves like a black-box once trained. But still, there is something quite amazing about what these models can do, even if I do not exactly understand how for now.
Like I said, it’s impressive. I don’t deny that.

I think the reason blockchain flopped is that it was a solution in want of a problem. It was an amazing technology that served no functional need. Already LLMs have done something useful: Claude brought the fraction of zeroes satisfying the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2% for the Riemann hypothesis and ChatGPT found a counterexample to the Erdos unit distance conjecture. I'm not saying AGI is around the corner, but we are already well past anything blockchain ever did.

aerh said:

But they don’t reason.

I think the "but they can't *" is often still within the self-assuring pattern. "Think", "reason", "feel", "empathize" etc are terms imbued with open anthropological notions and require precise definitions the very moment we try to discuss the epistemology of what these systems (and humans) do. Getting these definitions right is something even long-term researchers don't agree on, yet.

For practical matters, that's mostly an irrelevant objection. In the example I provided above, where I can get better didactic feedback than from the vast majority of professors I've ever had, it simply doesn't matter if the machine can/cannot empathize with my longing for learning. When I see LLM harness software retro-feed its output into its context window in order to build a coherent language flow, it doesn't matter if it's "reasoning" or not.

There's this video I really like in which Feynman talks about the capabilities of humans and machines: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ipRvjS7q1DI

When I say LLMs can’t reason, I don’t mean in a philosophical sense. They literally don’t use reason: GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models. The models that do have a reasoning mechanism have limits on what kinds of problems they can handle: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity.
TLDR, this tech can be useful for moderately complex problems but fails at higher complexities.

"I can construct a case where LLMs fall for biases or fail to reason carefully" is not at all equivalent to "LLMs literally do not use reason". The baseball-and-bat problem is something that humans will typically get right, with reason, on certain numbers:

A bat and a ball together cost $32.90. The bat costs $6.40 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?

most adults can answer correctly. The "original" problem,

A bat and a ball together cost $1.10. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?

with "only" numbers changed (like the GSM-Symbolic benchmark) typically gets people to use a fast-estimation path that causes most humans to get it wrong, including those well-educated in math. GSM-Symbolic is proof that "LLMs don't use reason", as much as the above is proof that humans don't use reason. (The consequent isn't insane: there are cases where humans do not use reason. This is fine.)

aerh said:

The models that do have a reasoning mechanism have limits on what kinds of problems they can handle: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity.

The experiment design of the second paper you mentioned is known to be flawed. Both papers are scoped empirical studies that need to be carefully interpreted, they are not evidence of the reasoning limitation of transformer-based architectures in a universal/principal sense.

The concensus of the industry is that there are still great reasoning potential to explore in post-training stage, even with smaller models. Transformer-based architectures have their share of limitations, but not at the scale or difficulty level in these two papers.

There are many factors in play, so if one experiences a limitation, the cause is not immediately obvious: it could be how the agent (model+harness) was set up and interacted with, or how the model was trained for the use case, or many other reasons. Nowadays with frontier models, it is usually fair to assume, the cause is how we use it. (EDIT: And it is no longer safe to assume that any limitations of models today, will still be there in a year, or even months.)

Back to the essay, my takeaway is that LLMs are just one of the new methods mathemacians should be encouraged to use, and mathemacians still have a lot to contribute to the advances of mathematics, and will find out about their/our own value with more use of new methods (not limited to LLMs or broader AI technologies), other than just "being supplanted by AI, there is nothing left for us to do but look for a meaningful residue", and going through grief.

So I'm deeply touched by the positive perspective in this essay, in contrast to digesting AI results, or the crisis of trust and the education of next generations.
